title: The ordinary believer
hook: history is kings, but faith was carried by mothers, farmers and traders

segments.voice: Yesterday, knowledge was worship: the stars and the body studied as ilm, with the right intention, as a way of turning to God. Your line was study as prayer. What did you learn, and what was it for? Day one thousand fifty.

In Medina, in the Prophet's mosque, someone used to sweep the floor. The narrator of the hadith isn't even sure whether it was a man or a woman. One day the Prophet, peace be upon him, noticed the sweeper was missing and asked. People told him the sweeper had died and been buried. They hadn't thought it worth telling him. He asked them to show him the grave, and he went and prayed there. A sweeper whose name the record didn't keep, and a prophet who walked to the grave. Today: the ordinary believer.
screen: `SOMEONE SWEPT THE MOSQUE.` → `BURIED, UNNOTICED.` → `HE WENT TO THE GRAVE.`

segments.voice: First, notice what that story in Sahih al-Bukhari keeps and what it drops. It keeps the work and the visit. It drops the name. Second, look at who the chronicles name. Caliphs, sultans, generals, the occasional famous scholar. That's what chroniclers wrote down. But a faith doesn't survive on coronations. Someone had to teach a child the opening surah at a kitchen table. Someone had to stop work at the edge of a field when the time for prayer came. Someone had to carry the prayer across the sea in a trader's head, and keep it in a port town far from home. Mothers, farmers, traders, sweepers. Mostly unnamed. Third, the tradition itself points the light at them. A hadith in Sahih Muslim reports the Prophet saying that God does not look at your bodies or your appearance, but at your hearts and your deeds. Not your title. Not your wealth. Fourth, take that lens back through the reigns this path has named. The bond Ibn Khaldun wrote about lives or dies in ordinary friendships. Even yesterday's scholars learned their first letters from someone. Every time this path told you a ruler's name, there were unnamed people under that reign, raising children, working fields, teaching the prayer. The history books are thin on them. The faith isn't.
screen: `THE SWEEPER OF THE MOSQUE.` · `CHRONICLES NAME THE KINGS.` · `GOD LOOKS AT HEARTS AND DEEDS.` · `UNDER EVERY REIGN, UNNAMED HANDS.`

segments.voice: The practice: thank an ordinary believer. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who passed something good on to you, and who will never be in a history book. Whoever taught you a prayer, or how to be kind, or how to keep going. A grandparent, a teacher, an aunt, a neighbor, a coach. See their face, their hands, the room where it happened. Stay with them until the bell. If you pray, you can ask God's mercy for them by name. If they're living, decide how you'll tell them. The bell holds the time.
Sahih Muslim, the hadith collection that keeps the Prophet's saying that God looks at hearts and deeds, not bodies or titles. Today's word.
Your line: ordinary hands carried it. Today, thank one person who passed something on to you, out loud or in writing. Day one thousand fifty.

howItsDone: Muslims often learn their first surahs and the prayer from parents and grandparents at home, and some pray for the forgiveness of their teachers and parents by name.

fork.setup: you're the Prophet. you learn that the person who swept your mosque died and was buried, and nobody told you. what do you do?

send a message of thanks to the family later.
fork.reveal: the hadith in Bukhari says he asked them to show him the grave, and went and prayed there.

trapdoor: what you thought: the history of a faith is the history of its rulers.
what it means: the faith was carried by unnamed mothers, farmers, traders and sweepers.
what a scholar hears: the hadith of the mosque sweeper in Bukhari, where even the narrator is unsure of the sweeper's name or sex, and Muslim's hadith that God looks at hearts and deeds.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 458 (the person who swept the mosque; the Prophet prays at the grave)
Sahih Muslim 2564 (Allah does not look at your bodies or forms but at your hearts and deeds)

notes: Bukhari 458 paraphrased: the narration describes the sweeper as 'a black man or a black woman' (narrator unsure); the script keeps the uncertainty and omits the description. Confirm number and whether the burial 'at night' detail is in this narration (it is in Muslim 956 and some Bukhari versions).
Week end (days 1044–1050): the teach's fourth turn looks back at the week.
